entry.title: The Stoic Lesson From Epictetus: You Can’t Make Someone Love You

link.title: The Stoic Lesson From Epictetus: You Can’t Make Someone Love You

entry.content:
I Wish Someone Told Me This in My 20s

Some things are within our power, while others are not. Within our power are opinion, motivation, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever is of our own doing; not within our power are our body, our property, reputation, office, and, in a word, whatever is not of our own doing. — Epictetus

This is the Dichotomy of Control — the core Stoic idea that real peace comes from putting your energy only into what’s actually yours: your thoughts, your effort, your actions. Everything else — how people see you, what they feel about you or other people, how things turn out — was never yours to begin with.

I learned this the hard way, and I mean the hard way.

Growing up, I was fed love stories from movies and dramas. The girl always starts out cold, the guy chases anyway, and persistence eventually wins her over. There is some truth to it. But not as much as I expected. When I was twenty-something, hot-blooded, with unstable emotions, you get one very confident, very wrong conclusion: if I want her, I just need to try hard enough, long enough, and eventually she’ll come around. Oh boy, how wrong I was.

When I was in my 20s, there was this one girl I liked. I really liked her. She was from my circle of friends, unofficially introduced to me because her circle overlapped with mine. Smart, pretty, always smiling. I’d bet anyone who met her liked her.

So eventually I started to pursue her. And she said no. Friends only, she said. But the movies and dramas say otherwise. If I chase long enough, if I’m persistent enough, she’ll eventually fall for me. And that’s exactly what I did — because I thought, yeah, I can do this, I can control the outcome.

Oh boy, if only I’d read what Marcus Aurelius wrote back then:

If you are distressed by anything external, the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it — and this you have the power to revoke at any moment.

So I chased and chased. Refused to take no as final. Convinced myself she was the one, and that belief consumed me so completely it blocked out the obvious truth staring me in the face.

In the movies, the girl eventually falls for the guy because he “put in the effort” and never surrendered. In my case, however, she never did.

Looking back now, at 40, I actually cringe. If I could go back in time, I’d be genuinely embarrassed at what I did. Like, a lot.

Here’s what took me two decades to understand: chasing someone who doesn’t want to be caught isn’t romantic, it’s just a waste of time and energy dressed up as devotion. If she likes you, she likes you. If she doesn’t, you could die trying and she still wouldn’t. No amount of effort converts a “no” into a “yes,” because her feelings were never a project I could work on — they were hers, not mine, not ever.

The idea that she’ll eventually come around only exists in the movies. In real life, it’s rarely the case.

That’s the part I got backwards for years. I was pouring everything I had into the one thing I had zero control over, while barely paying attention to the only things I actually did control — my own actions, my own growth, my own choices about who deserved my energy in the first place.

And it’s not just relationships. It’s everything in life.

Epictetus said it plainly: Within our power are opinion, motivation, desire, aversion — in a word, whatever is of our own doing.

The outcome of a game. Whether you get the job after the interview. People’s opinion of you. Even the loss of someone you love. All of it is beyond our control. There’s no switch we can flick to overturn the result into what we wanted.

All of it works the same way — you control the effort, not the result. Chasing the result instead of owning the effort is how you end up 40 years old, looking back at your 20s, wincing.

Letting go isn’t giving up. It’s finally putting your energy where it was always supposed to go — into what’s actually yours to control.

It’s not resignation, it’s redirection: the same fire I used to burn chasing something that was never mine, now goes into the things that are — how I show up, what I build, who I choose to become. That’s the only chase that was ever worth running.
entry.summary: Spent your 20s chasing things you couldn't control? Discover the harsh, liberating Stoic lessons from Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius on letting go.

entry.title: 10 Marcus Aurelius Inspirational Quotes To Strengthen You Through Bad Day

link.title: 10 Marcus Aurelius Inspirational Quotes To Strengthen You Through Bad Day

entry.content:
Bad days happen. Everybody has to go through them one way or another. But rather than drowning yourself in negative thoughts, you can choose to toughen up, face the chaos, and push through.

If you are dealing with a rough day right now, let these 10 practical quotes from Stoic Emperor Marcus Aurelius provide some comfort and perspective.

1. Reclaim Your Mental Control

You have power over your mind – not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.

A lot of the time, we suffer more in our minds and imaginations than in real life. Embrace your inner strength and block out the outside noise. That is how you find true inner peace.

2. Take It Moment by Moment

Do not disturb yourself by thinking of the whole of your life… As closely as possible, check each moment as it comes.

Don’t let the weight of the entire week, month, or year crush you today. Break the day down into manageable chunks. Focus entirely on navigating the exact minute you are in right now.

3. Guard Your Peace Against Toxic People

When you wake up in the morning, tell yourself: The people I deal with today will be meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous, and surly… None of them can hurt me.

Yes, difficult people are the worst—but let them be. That is their level, and you don’t need to lower your standards just to meet theirs. Their bad attitude cannot change who you are.

4. Choose High Standards Over Revenge

The best revenge is to be unlike him who performed the injury.

When someone treats you poorly, the ultimate victory isn’t hitting back. It’s choosing not to act like them. Stay calm, stay classy, and move on.

5. Refuse to Play the Victim

Reject your sense of injury and the injury itself disappears.

A bad day only wins if you let it convince you that you’ve been defeated. If you refuse to feel like a victim, the situation loses all its power over your mood.

6. Flip the Problem on its Head

The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.

When a roadblock ruins your plans, look for the hidden pivot. Use the obstacle as a chance to test your patience, find a creative workaround, or try a completely new path.

7. Find Your Inner Escape Hatch

People look for retreats for themselves, in the country, by the coast, or in the hills… There is nowhere that a person can find a more peaceful and trouble-free retreat than in his own mind.

You don’t need an expensive vacation or a physical escape to find peace. Close your eyes, take a breath, and step away from the chaos by anchoring yourself internally.

8. Remember That This Too Shall Pass

Time is a river, a fierce torrent of things that come into being; no sooner is a thing brought to sight than it is swept away and another takes its place, and this too will be swept away.

No matter how brutal today feels, it only lasts 24 hours. The bad traffic, the rough meetings, and the stress will all eventually be swept away by time.

9. Stop Overthinking and Just Act

Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one.

When a bad day causes mental paralysis, stop overanalyzing the problem. Quit worrying about how things “should” be, and simply take the next right step.

10. Zoom Out and Look at the Big Picture

Dwell on the beauty of life. Watch the stars, and see yourself running with them.

When you feel overwhelmed by small, frustrating details, look up. Remind yourself of the massive, beautiful universe out there. It makes today’s headaches feel thankfully small.

entry.title: Why Stoic Philosophy Still Matters in 2026

link.title: Why Stoic Philosophy Still Matters in 2026

entry.content:
There is a reason Marcus Aurelius wrote Meditations for himself — not for us. He was trying to remember, every single day, the principles that kept him grounded as one of the most powerful men in the world.

That’s the thing about Stoicism. It was never meant to be a philosophy for the comfortable. It was built for pressure.

What Stoicism Actually Is

Most people misunderstand Stoicism as emotional suppression — the idea that you should feel nothing, endure everything, and keep a blank face through suffering. That’s not it.

Stoicism is the practice of distinguishing between what is within your control and what is not — and directing your energy accordingly.

“You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realise this, and you will find strength.” — Marcus Aurelius

The external world — other people’s opinions, the economy, the weather, other people’s choices — none of it is yours to control. What is yours: your response, your attention, your values, your effort.

Why It Resonates Now

We live in an era of information overload, constant comparison, and manufactured urgency. Social media has industrialised anxiety. Every notification is a small demand on your attention. Every headline is engineered to provoke a reaction.

Stoicism cuts through all of it with a simple question: Is this within my control?

If yes — act. If no — release it.

That’s not passivity. That’s clarity.

Three Stoic Practices Worth Adopting

1. Morning reflection. Before the day starts, spend five minutes asking: what might go wrong today, and how will I respond with integrity?

2. Negative visualisation. Briefly imagine losing what you value most. Not to be morbid — but to appreciate what you have and prepare yourself emotionally.

3. Evening review. At night, ask: where did I fall short today? Where did I act with virtue? No self-punishment, just honest accounting.

These aren’t grand gestures. They’re small, daily disciplines — exactly what Stoicism was always about.

The Stoics didn’t promise happiness. They promised something more durable: the ability to remain yourself, regardless of what the world throws at you.

That’s worth more than ever right now.
entry.summary: Stoicism isn't about suppressing emotion — it's about understanding what you can and cannot control. Here's why it's more relevant than ever.
